question.text: An adult drinks a cup of coffee that contains $110$ mg of caffeine, and each hour the amount of caffeine in their body decreases by $15\%.$ To the nearest integer, how much caffeine will be left in their system after $11$ hours?
question.explanation:
The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay rate $r$) is

\[ y = a(1-r)^t. \]

In our case, we have the following:

  • $a=110$ is the initial amount of caffeine in the adult's body.

  • $r = 0.15$ is the decay rate ($15\%$ expressed as a decimal).

  • $t=$ the time, in hours.

Therefore, the correct expression for $y$ is

\begin{align*} y &= 110\cdot (1-0.15)^{t}\\ &=110\cdot (0.85)^{t}. \end{align*}

Evaluating the expression for $t=11$ hours, we get

\[ y(11) = 110\cdot (0.85)^{11} \approx 18. \]

Hence, after $11$ hours, there will be $18$ mg of caffeine left in their system.

question.text: Austin's average monthly profit has been decreasing at a rate of $6\%$ every year. If he initially recorded an average monthly profit of $\$58\,000$, then which function correctly represents $p(t),$ Austin's average monthly profit since the start of the decline?
question.explanation:
The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay rate $r$) is

\[ p(t) = a(1-r)^t. \]

In our case, we have the following:

  • $a=58\,000$ is the initial average monthly profit.

  • $r = 0.06$ is the decay rate ($6\%$ expressed as a decimal).

  • $t=$ the time, in years.

Therefore, the correct expression for $p$ is

\[ p(t)= 58\,000\cdot (1 - 0.06)^{t} = 58\,000\cdot (0.94)^{t}. \]

question.text:
A lake currently has a depth of $320$ feet. The depth of the lake is expected to decrease by one-tenth every year.

The function $d(t)$ models the depth of the lake after $t$ years and is given by

\[ d(t)=320\cdot \left(\textrm{___}\right)^{t}. \]

What number is missing?
question.explanation:
If the depth reduces by $\dfrac 1 {10}$ every month, then $\dfrac{9}{10}$ of the depth remains every year. So the decay factor is $\dfrac{9}{10}.$

The formula for exponential decay (in terms of a decay factor $b$) is

\[ d(t) = ab^t. \]

In our case, we have the following:

  • $a=320$ is the initial depth.

  • $b = \dfrac{9}{10}$ is the decay factor.

  • $t=$ the time, in years.

Therefore, the correct expression for $d(t)$ is

\[ d(t)= 320 \cdot \left(\dfrac{9}{10}\right)^{t}. \]

So the missing number is $\dfrac{9}{10}.$
